newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr unsettled by rate confusion.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr unsettled by rate confusion.

text.p: The Australian dollar stumbled from early highs at the close Tuesday as a failure to clear 79 cent resistance prompted profit-taking.
Traders said the market was also been unsettled by reports Treasurer Peter Costello had said another cut in domestic interest rates could not be ruled out.

The bald report was not entirely borne out by his quoted comments, however, since he merely noted the Reserve Bank had not expressely ruled out an easing but rather said current policy settings were appropriate. It was up to the reader to interpret that, he added.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar had edged back to US$0.7875/80 from an early US$0.7897 high, but was still up on Monday's late US$0.7860/65.
The currency had looked ready to bust higher early after bids from local, U.S. and Swiss names rescued it from under US$0.7860 offshore.
The local market was not keen to chase it higher, however, given there was much talk of fresh offers lurking above 79 and the reluctance turned into profit taking as the day wore on.
The range-trading mentality was reinforced when the yen firmed on upbeat Japanese data and the Costello report arrived.
Japan reported private machinery orders had jumped 11.8 percent in January which was well above expectations and continued an improving trend in recent releases.

Traders said the data reminded the market that Japanese rates could not stay at record lows for ever and prompted a knee jerk yen buying which saw the local dollar dip to 95.55/65 yen from an early 95.92/02.

This was not far from Monday's late 95.65/75, however, and they noted the Japanese bond market had not seemed too perturbed with the key 10-year JGB yield falling to a record low today at 2.320 percent.
The comparable Australia yield was 7.80 percent, which also happened to be the highest in the entire OECD including countries such as Italy which have higher inflation and deeper debt problems.

Traders said there was little talk anymore of large scale yen/A$ samurai bond redemptions, which had fuelled heavy A$ selling in January and February, and there was even the chance of new Japanese demand once the financial year-end was over.
There was a hint of this today with Nomura launching a 15 billion yen/A$ reverse samurai bond -- it pays interest in A$ and principal in yen -- the second since late February.
Despite Costello's admonitions the local market continued to believe another RBA rate cut was off the agenda and were comforted in their conviction by partial labour data today.
Figures compiled by the ANZ on the number of job advertisements in major newspapers showed a rise of 1.8 percent in February on top of a 3.3 percent gain in January.
"The improving trend in job advertising bodes well for a continuation of employment growth over coming months," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Tony Meer.
That in turn promised to buoy consumer spending and ensure January's rebound in retail sales was more than a one-off.
"Today's data helps to further consolidate our view that monetary policy is currently on hold with the direction of the next move likely to be up," he said.
Dollar bulls hoped his assessment would be confirmed by consumer cofidence data Wednesday and the official jobs data for February which are due the day after.
The Westpac consumer sentiment index fell a sharp 7.9 percent in Febuary and analysts are looking for a bounce in March as commercial banks slashed their mortgage rates recently.
Median forecasts for jobs are for a rise of 10,000 following January's firm 28,400 gain. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
